picks.rationale: I put bevacizumab first because it is the option whose safety I can actually predict: approved since 2014, two large 1L phase-3 trials (GOG-218 n=1873, ICON7 n=1528) with more than a decade of post-marketing follow-up, and the patient is already on it and tolerating it. Neither named veto is triggered. The grade 2+ hypertension rate (22.9% vs 7.2% in GOG-218) has a well-worn management algorithm, and bowel-wall disruption stayed at 2.6%. My one real caution is VTE/bleeding given her high VTE history and prior IVC filter, so I would keep her on the established BP and bleeding monitoring rather than escalate.
primary_concerns: VTE and bleeding risk against the patient's high VTE history and prior IVC filter, though no neuropathy or myelosuppression veto applies
PFS benefit only; OS was not improved in the GOG-218 overall population and the ICON7 OS gain was confined to the high-risk subset

picks.rationale: Niraparib is the strongest efficacy fit on paper: PRIMA (n=733) enrolled all-comers with no BRCA mutation or validated HRD score required, HR 0.62 overall, and it is FDA-approved on-label, so a BRCA-WT genomically-unstable tumor qualifies cleanly. I rank it second rather than first only because it trips her stated severe-myelosuppression veto head-on: grade 3+ thrombocytopenia 28.7%, anemia 31%, neutropenia 12.8%. The individualized starting dose by body weight and baseline platelet count blunts that risk but does not erase it, and her baseline WBC is already 3.5. I can be talked up to rank 1 if a hematology-supported dose plan and a clear cytopenia-management pathway are documented.
primary_concerns: Triggers the patient's severe myelosuppression / febrile neutropenia veto: grade 3+ thrombocytopenia 28.7%, anemia 31%
Baseline WBC 3.5 narrows the marrow reserve before any drug-related cytopenia

picks.rationale: Letrozole is the gentlest option in front of the board: oral, once-daily, no infusion burden, and it trips none of her vetoes, which suits the 70-79 age band and her oral-therapy preference. The catch is the evidence base. The supporting data are a non-randomized retrospective comparison nested in a translational ER-expression study (ROBINS-I serious), and her PR-negativity predicts a more modest response than the ER-positive (~80% nuclei) reading alone suggests. I keep it on the list as a low-toxicity add-on or later-line choice, not as a substitute for a maintenance regimen with randomized backing. Arthralgia and bone-density loss on prolonged aromatase inhibition are the main things to watch.
primary_concerns: Evidence is a non-randomized retrospective series (ROBINS-I serious), not the randomized data the higher-ranked options carry
PR-negativity tempers the expected endocrine magnitude despite ~80% ER positivity

notes: Ranking is deliberately tolerability-first. The single most decision-relevant workup remains a validated genomic-instability score (Myriad MyChoice CDx GIS >=42 or FDA equivalent): if it comes back >=42 the patient becomes PAOLA-1 eligible and olaparib + bevacizumab (HR 0.33 HRD-positive; 0.43 in the BRCA-non-mutated HRD-positive subgroup) moves into contention, though I would weigh that combination's ~57% grade 3+ AE rate and added hypertension against her VTE history before endorsing it. Below 42 she is HRD-negative and the all-comer PARP question stays with niraparib. I did not rank the early-phase PI3K or MAP2K4 baskets or GEN-1; they sit outside a conservative round-1 pick on safety-characterization grounds, and SOLO1 olaparib monotherapy is foreclosed by BRCA-WT status.
